en: Preface to the Re-engraved *Chan-yuan ch’üan* The Way cannot manifest itself;
it must rely on persons to manifest it. Although their manifestations differ, the Way has never been different.
If they were truly different, they would not be the Way—just as with Confucius’s "one thread" (*yiguan*).
The non-action of Lao Dan and the emptiness and stillness of the Śākya school differ in person but are identical in principle.
This is the proof. Moreover,
since both the Chan and Teaching schools originated from the Buddha— Chan being the Buddha’s mind—
how could they be at odds?
The teachings are the very words of the Buddha;
how could there be a contradiction between his heart and his speech?
Alas, the time since the Sage passed away is now remote.
Their lineages differ.
Those of the Teaching regard Chan as a dark realization;
those of Chan view the Teaching as gradual cultivation.
They have not attained impartiality regarding clarity and obscurity,
nor do they know where to find certainty between the sudden and gradual approaches;
they alternately revile one another as if they were mortal enemies.
It is not merely a matter of empty words being drummed forth;
it has moreover been committed to writing in scrolls and volumes.
The ways of the world are declining day by day.
What, then, shall we do with these defects?
In the past, Master Guifeng was troubled by this;
he consequently compiled the writings and aphorisms of the various patriarchs of both the Exegetical and Chan traditions that accorded in their essential meaning.
He compiled them into a single book titled *The Explanations of the Sources of Chan* (*Chanyuan zhuiquan*) to instruct the world.
This shall cause the scholars of both houses to know that there is but one Buddha and no second path,
and that the four rivers have no different flavors;
thus their words shall return to harmony.
That the alliance was never again broken was due to the merit of Yuan Quan;
how could his achievement be easily measured?
Whenever I observe this corruption in the south, it is particularly severe.
How can we obtain someone who possesses such a book to thoroughly cleanse these old habits?
May all together give rise to new and wholesome thoughts; reflecting upon this, I have reached this conclusion.
There has never been a time when I did not set aside my meal to sigh in admiration.
Now, Master President Xuetang appears to have attained some profound realization.
He specially donated surplus cloth to restore and renew the woodblocks so that they might be widely circulated.
He traveled a thousand li to send me this letter, requesting that I compose a preface for it.
Since the former Prime Minister, Duke Pei, has already provided a preface,
what person like myself would dare to overstep him in this manner and incur the censure of the wise?
Nevertheless, this book is that which I have cherished and admired throughout my life.
How fortunate that my name is inscribed among these!
Therefore, I do not decline.
In the seventh month of the seventh year of the Dade era, Wudaivai of Jianyan Wuwai at Kunshan composed this preface.
Preface to the Re-engraved *Chan-yuan ch'üan* The *Chan-yuan ch'üan* (Exposition of the Source of Chan) was composed by the Tang Dynasty Master Guifeng.
The Way of the Buddha is vast, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Yet it becomes as subtle as a fine mote of dust;
neither existent nor empty,
with no interior and no exterior.
Later students of Chan, whose resolve was to exhaustively realize the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa),
regarded words and phrases as pedantic and trivial.
Those who establish the teachings strive to verify the true exegesis,
yet they treat emptiness and quiescence as mere empty rhetoric.
To treat them as separate is a different perspective;
it does not clarify their underlying unity.
How could this be the fundamental nature of the Buddha’s Way?
Thereupon, he taught three types of instruction and three schools of Chan meditation:
namely, explaining characteristics based on nature,
which consists of quelling delusions and cultivating the mind.
By breaking through appearances to reveal the nature,
one reaches a state of total cessation where there is no place for reliance;
thus, the true mind is manifested.
This directly clarifies the nature of the mind:
though the Yangtze and Han rivers flow in different directions, they both return to the ocean of wisdom;
though sour and salty flavors differ in their seasoning, they together lead to the taste of dhyāna.
As for the distinction between the schools of Emptiness and Nature,
and the difference between sudden and gradual cultivation,
none fail to converge upon their ultimate aim and reveal perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, fearing that those of later learning might easily be deluded and find it difficult to attain awakening,
I have also drawn diagrams alongside the text, marking them in vermilion and ink,
from initial sudden enlightenment up to the attainment of Buddhahood.

The ten stages from "not being self-aware" to "receiving retribution" constitute purity. The ten stages [from "arousing the thought of enlightenment"] to "receiving retribution" constitute defilement.
The source of purity and defilement depends upon the sage and the ordinary person;
the mental phenomena fully possess both the true and the false.
This is called the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
If one does not awaken, one is deluded regarding the truth and pursues the false, wandering through saṃsāra for kalpas.
If one awakens suddenly, one abandons the false and returns to the truth, following it toward liberation.
Nevertheless, students must understand that the teaching on True Suchness (tathatā) is like a finger pointing at the moon.
If one further sees the moon and realizes that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon,
then both the designation and the diagram are forgotten.
Both the ignorant and the wise equally possess Prajñā;
both the defiled and the pure realize Bodhi.
Thus it was at Mount Nanyue, Tiantai, Nan-sheng, and Bei-xiu.
This is no different from the fundamental tenets of the Dharma’s arrival in the East;
how, then, can there be any distinction between Chan and the Teachings?
During the Dazhong era of the Tang dynasty...
Prime Minister Pei Xiu composed a preface for it and personally inscribed this illustration,
entrusting it to Yanchang Temple in Jinzhou.
The lineage was subsequently transmitted only to Master Jing;
it was then transmitted a second time to Master Xuanqi.
Thus, the teachings were practiced in the regions of Min, Xiang, Wu, and Yue.
In the twelfth year of the Zhizhi era of our dynasty,
Emperor Shizu presided over the Guanghan Hall and requested an inquiry into the essential meanings of Chan and the Teachings.
The Imperial Preceptor and various venerable elders compared [the text] with Chan-yuan’s commentary;
the Emperor was delighted and ordered it to be carved into printing blocks for circulation in the world.
Twenty-nine years later, in the Great Virtue Gui-mao year,
his dharma successor, Zen Master Xuedang Ren,
was granted imperial edict to travel to Mount Wutai.
On the return journey, passing through Datong,
I obtained a painting calligraphed by the Chan Master Jue of Jinshi Qian’an,
which further enhanced my research and verification.
I have compiled this refined and elegant work to transmit it to distant lands,
so that Master Guifeng may investigate the truth and manifest the orthodox teaching,
fulfilling his intention to transform and guide the deluded masses.
It shall never fall into decline.
How can its benefit be measured?
Wenyuan has maintained a relationship of external friendship with the Master.
Thereupon, he expressed his sympathetic joy and praise, arranging the sequence of the discourse and recording it at the beginning of this volume.

Written on the first day of the intercalary month of this year by Deng Wenyuan of Baxi, Acting Hanlin Scholar, Willing Official of the Second Grade, Joint Director of the Bureau of Imperial Edicts, and Compiler of the Court of Imperial History.
Preface to the Re-engraved *Chan-yuan ch’üan* Master Xuedang was of heroic and far-reaching intellect,
and his practice and realization were perfectly integrated.
He delighted in cultivation and conduct.
Yue Shi-yu once said to me: "I have long been troubled by those in the world who study Buddhism."

Failing to investigate the causes behind the Tathāgata’s establishment of his teachings, they have falsely clung to the notions of emptiness and existence, competing over the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles.
Whether speaking of the Sudden or the Gradual, of Chan or Vinaya, they have engaged in endless,
fragmented disputes for over a thousand years.
It is as if one were to protect their father’s feet only to cause them to suffer fully from illness;
although I have encountered one or two like-minded companions who might have been able to enlighten me,
I regret that I could not inform every family and household.
Fortunately, I have obtained the *Chan-yuan ch'üan* (Exposition of the Source of Chan) composed by Kueifeng.
Its prose is profound and elegant, and its purport is precise and pertinent;
it fully recounts what I previously found troubling and explains the reasons why those difficulties arose.
Furthermore, I have prepared a diagram illustrating that the single reality of the mind contains three great meanings:
through ignorance, various defiled phenomena falsely arise;
by relying on the methods of cultivation and abandonment, one attains realization and entry into the principle.
To grasp the main principles and summarize the essentials is like pointing at something in the palm of one's hand.
Formerly, in the first month of spring in the twelfth year of the Zhiyuan era,
during a period of leisure from the myriad affairs of state, Emperor Shizu—
He invited the Imperial Preceptor to Mount Qionghua Island;
the Grand Guardian Wenzheng, Lord Liu, was also present.
Thereupon, he summoned the venerable elders residing in the capital to inquire about the points of divergence and convergence between the various Chan and doctrinal schools.
The late master Xianan Yungong and seven others were consequently selected to correspond with the *Guifeng Chan-yuan Quanwen* (Gui Peak’s Commentary on the Source of Chan),
which fully satisfied the Emperor’s wishes.
At that time, my late master entrusted his younger brother, Master Shuangquan Tai, to compose a record for it,
and further commanded Xuedang to carve the woodblocks for its circulation. As for myself,
I have traveled about to consult various masters of the different quarters.
I have not yet had the leisure to reach this point.
Previously, while at the Yunzhong and Puen Xingguo Monasteries, I obtained one copy from each.
Later, I was at the quarters of the Abbot of Wanshou Monastery in the capital.
Furthermore, we obtained the definitive edition printed and promulgated throughout the realm in the eighth year of the Qingning era (1092) by Empress Dowager Chongtian of the Liao dynasty;
having compared it with the literary version for correction, we intend to carve it into printing blocks to ensure its transmission for all eternity.
"I request that you speak a word so as to fulfill the late master's遗志 (unfulfilled aspirations).
Upon hearing this, I said with joy:
'Now, your heart is precisely the same as Master Guifeng’s heart of concern for the world.'"
However, without these writings, there would be no means to dispel their delusions;
without ensuring their transmission endures, there would be no way to benefit the multitude.
Thus, when scholars behold them, their afflictions would not be cast off and liberation would not arise.
What benefit would there be?
Regarding what the ancients called the "four difficulties," three of them are not present now; only one remains.
Therefore, may those students from all quarters who study this work not fail the two masters' intention to propagate the Dharma and benefit sentient beings;
may they read and contemplate it with their whole hearts until their emotions are dispelled and understanding arises.
Like King Liang who, holding the six reins, gallops along the broad thoroughfare,
or like the Master who boards the vessel of Prajñā to reach the other shore—
how could there be anyone who does not arrive?

Preface to the General Introduction to the *Chan Yuan Zhu Quan Ji* (The Collection of Explanations on the Sources of Chan), composed by Jia Ruzhou, Court Attendant of the Hanlin Academy, Grand Master of the Imperial Retinue, and Joint Editor of the National History. Recorded by Pei Xiu, Prefectural Governor of Mianzhou during the Tang Dynasty, who compiled the collected works of Master Guifeng and provided this general preface for the *Chan Yuan Zhu Quan* as the Chan Canon.
Pei Xiu of Hedong said, "This is unprecedented!
Since the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he has established teachings according to the capacities of beings."
The Bodhisattva, appearing in the intervals between births, prescribes medicine according to the illness;
thus, throughout the various periods of the Buddha's teaching,
he opened three gates of varying depth.
With a single mind of true purity,
he expounded the distinct dharmas of nature and characteristics;
thus were the two masters, Ma and Long.
Both propagated the teachings of the Great Tamer (the Buddha),
yet their doctrines on emptiness differed;
such were the two masters, Neng and Xiu.
While both transmit the mind of the Dharma,
they differ in their sudden and gradual transmissions;
Heze directly points to knowledge and vision.
In Jiangxi, everything is true;
at Tiantai, one relies exclusively on the three contemplations;
at Niutou, there is not a single dharma.
Furthermore, emptiness and existence mutually negate one another;
truth and falsehood encompass each other;
they are taken away by reversal and grasped through conformity.
The esoteric is taught through the exoteric;
thus, the traditions in India and China are truly numerous.
This is because illnesses have a thousand sources, and medicines arise in many varieties.
They adapt to circumstances and accord with capacities, so they cannot be treated as identical.
Although they are all gateways to realization and awakening,
they are each entirely the true and correct Way.
Furthermore, among the various schools, those that are universal are few while those that are restrictive are many;
thus, over the past few decades, the teacher-disciple tradition has deteriorated even further,
with individuals treating their own lineage of transmission as the sole door and window to the truth.
Each opened their own school,
taking the sutras and śāstras as their weapons to attack one another.
Sentiment shifts and changes according to the armor-maker and the arrow-maker. Mencius said:
"Is the maker of arrows not more benevolent than the maker of armor?"
The maker of armor only fears that it might fail to protect from injury;
the maker of arrows only fears that they might fail to inflict injury.
This is simply because of the nature of the arts in which they have been trained.
Nowadays, scholars merely follow their respective schools, mutually disparaging one another.
[Regarding] the character "函" (hán): *Táng yùn* (Rhymes of the Táng).
"From the golden helmet" refers to armor.
According to the *Rites of Zhou* (*Zhouli*): [text continues].
"The maker of armor" refers to one who constructs armor; in ancient script,
this term was often written with a single character.
Therefore, Mencius also merely established his own method to rank people as high or low;
when right and wrong become so entangled that they cannot be distinguished,
then the various teachings and schools of the World-Honored One and the Bodhisattvas of the past—
This is sufficient to give rise to disputes and cause later generations to increase their afflictions and illnesses;
what benefit could there possibly be in this?
After a long time, Master Guifeng sighed and said:
"I am living at such a time that I cannot remain silent. When Confucius edited the *Shi* and *Shu* and rectified the rites and music, he did so because he had no other choice."
Therefore, I transmit but do not create;
this is because the Sage values the Way and does not value its traces.
My intention is that I have long cultivated the Buddha-dharma of our own school.
Now, to suddenly bring these various schools into harmony—
how could this be intended as a mere establishment of my own legacy? It was simply unavoidable.
It is precisely at this juncture that harmony must be achieved; thus, the threefold teachings of the Tathāgata were used to seal the threefold Dharma-gates of the Chan school.
To melt bottles, platters, hairpins, and bracelets into a single piece of gold;
to stir buttermilk, cream, and clarified butter into a single flavor.
As Xunzi said: "When one shakes the collar, all that follows moves in accord."
It is like shaking the collar of a fur robe;

when the five fingers are bent and given a shake, those that follow in alignment are beyond counting. According to the *Huìyào*, those who come [to the assembly] move with a single, unified pace; the character "qù" (趨) is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*).
The "Brief Examples" (Lüe li) of the *Zhouyi* states:
"If one relies on the essential principles to observe what is yet to come,
then the six directions will converge like spokes in a wheel."
This is not yet sufficient.
The General Preface relies upon the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) to authenticate all other schools;
thus, even the hundred families are encompassed within it. Yet, fearing that students might still find this difficult to clarify, [the author] proceeds further.
Furthermore, it directly reveals the beginning and end of the source of the fundamental principle,
the union of the real and the false,
and the concealment and manifestation of emptiness.
The distinctions between the meanings of the Dharma;
the similarities and differences between the sudden and gradual approaches;
and the mutual reversals of concealment and revelation.
The depth and shallowness of the provisional and the real,
and the rightness or wrongness of the universal and the particular— these are clearly and earnestly expounded in the following passage of praise and narration.
In wishing for people to attain awakening, there is nothing better than to take them by the ear and inform them. As the *Mao Shi* says:
"It was not merely from face to face that I commanded; I spoke while taking hold of their ears.
At that time, [the sages] were distressed by those who did not cultivate virtue and fell into chaos and disorder.
I say that I did not speak to you face-to-face;
furthermore, I took you by the ear and raised you up,
addressing you right by your ear.
"You will never change your mind.
This means that his instructions were exceedingly earnest, as if pointing out one's palm to show it. As the *Analects* says:
"One who knows the principles of these matters, regarding the world at large..."
"How is it that you look at this? He pointed to his palm.
This means the Master spoke these words and pointed with his own hand to show his disciples, saying, "See this matter clearly."
Like an object held in the palm of one’s hand, it is easily understood; with sighs and groans he roars,
and with tender affection he entices— this below praises his compassionate concern,
like nurturing an infant.
I nourish them with milk and treat them with medicine,
for I fear that the seeds of the Buddha will perish or be injured. To lack even a small root of goodness and become an icchantika—
that is what constitutes such perishing and injury.
"To cradle and embrace him"— the *Mao Shi* says,
"She cradles me, she looks upon me," speaking of how a compassionate mother thinks of her young child.
He cradled me within his chest;
though he rose briefly to depart, he turned his head back to look at me, for his affection and regret were profound.

He was mindful of the perils of being swept away by water or consumed by fire, wishing to take us by the hand and guide us through such calamities; he feared we might be deluded and ensnared by evil and trivial things, yet we already possessed the roots of goodness.
Furthermore, having distanced himself from the five desires,
he feared that [beings] would not enter the Mahāyāna; thus, he shook them and dispersed them,
lamenting the tenacity of their strife.
The Great Light cannot dispel the gloom of the long night;

a compassionate mother cannot protect her child after her own passing. The following passage laments that compassion and wisdom are identical to those of the Buddha. Although the Sun of the Buddha is most radiant, [it cannot reach those beyond].
Only after obtaining my teacher can one turn the light back to illuminate the crooked;
though the Buddha’s compassion is universal, it is only through obtaining my teacher that its great benefit becomes even more extensive. Such is my teacher.
Holding up the sun of the Buddha, it shines its light with winding grace;
all doubts and obscurations are entirely dispelled.
Following the Buddha’s mind, the Great Compassion extends across all directions.
Having received benefit throughout the exhaustion of kalpas,
the World-Honored One is the master who expounds the teachings,
while our Teacher is the person who synthesizes those teachings.
The fundamental and the derivative support one another;
the distant and the near illuminate each other.

This may truly be called the fulfillment of all the capacities and tasks of the temporal teachings throughout a single kalpa, from the time the World-Honored One first expounded the Dharma until the present day.
Having brought them together and made them penetrate one another,
the task of service is finally completed.
Someone said:
Since the Tathāgata has never broadly disseminated this to all, yet now,
all at once, you have departed from its fundamental purpose and failed to maintain it;
you have abandoned its protective barriers and ceased to rely upon them.
"Would this not be a departure from the path of the secret treasury and the profound esoteric realization?
He replied, "In the assemblies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, the Buddha..."
They have also already been fused into a single flavor;
it is only that those who are deluded do not perceive it.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said,
"The Buddhas have secret words, but no secret treasury.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
The words of the Tathāgata are revealed, manifest, pure, and free from obscuration;
yet the foolish do not understand them.
It is kept as a secret treasury;
when the wise fully comprehend it, it is no longer called a "treasury"—
this is the proof.
Therefore, when the Way of the King flourishes, outer doors need not be closed, for defense lies with the barbarians;
when the Way of the Buddha is complete, all dharmas are held in total retention, for protection lies with Māras and externalists. The Perfect Teaching of Nirvāṇa harmonizes and unites all dharmas.
One need only distinguish between the teachings of Māra and the heterodox doctrines of external paths; one should not further allow one's emotions to interfere or take up arms amidst them.
Alas, for those who study hereafter!
One should place one's trust in the Buddha,
not in other persons; one should seek realization within the fundamental Dharma itself.
Do not grasp at or realize secondary practices.
General Preface:
Seal all schools with the Buddha’s words and illuminate partial teachings with the fundamental Dharma.

Therefore, I earnestly exhort you to have deep faith; if you can do so, you will not render in vain the merit of Guifeng’s diligent toil. "Alas, alas, my parents, who gave me life with such toil"—such is the virtue of our Master.
This goes even further than that.
Those who come after observe their methods yet feel no sense of sorrow or compassion;
they are no different from wood or stone.
Furthermore, you must take care of yourself.
